acts.label: Prologue
acts.desc: Host Ira Glass talks with Lauren Waterman, who's in the middle of a break-up right now and grappling with totally contradictory feelings.

acts.label: Act One
acts.desc:
In the wake of a break-up, writer Starlee Kine finds so much comfort in break-up songs that she decides to try and write one herself—even though she has no musical ability whatsoever. For some help, she goes to a rather surprising expert on the subject: Phil Collins.
Starlee was assisted in her efforts by musicians Joe McGinty and Julia Greenberg, who co-wrote the song featured in this story. Joe's album Kiss Me, Stupid with his band Baby Steps includes "This Song Is Three Days Old," also heard in Starlee's story. He is the co-author with Hally McGehean of the musical “ Upping My Numbers. ” Julia writes songs and composes musical theater in Brooklyn. For more stories by Starlee, check out her podcast Mystery Show.

songs.t: If You Ever Need a Stranger (To Sing at Your Wedding)

acts.title: Dr. Phil

acts.label: Act Two
acts.desc:
Eight-year-old Betsy Walter goes on a campaign to understand her parents' divorce — a campaign that takes her to school guidance counselors, children's book authors, and the mayor of New York City.
The interview with Betsy first aired on NPR's All Things Considered —in 1987, when a young Ira Glass was a producer there.
acts.title: But Why?

acts.label: Act Three
acts.desc:
Ira talks with divorce mediator Barry Berkman about why it's bad when the justice system gets involved in a break-up.
Barry specializes in matrimonial law and is a member of The New York Association of Collaborative Professionals, which he helped found.
acts.title: Let No Court Put Asunder

acts.label: Act Four
acts.desc:
What divorce looks like from the dog's point of view.
This monologue was performed by Merrill Markoe and recorded at Un-Cabaret in Los Angeles. Merrill's most recent book of essays is Cool, Calm and Contentious.
acts.title: Divorce Is Rrruuffff!
